'''Atlas Air Flight 3591''' was a scheduled domestic cargo flight between [[Miami International Airport]] and [[George Bush Intercontinental Airport]] in [[Houston]]. On February 23, 2019, the [[Boeing 767]] operating this flight crashed into [[Trinity Bay (Texas)|Trinity Bay]] during approach into Houston, killing the two crew members and single passenger on board. The accident occurred near [[Anahuac, Texas]], east of [[Houston]], shortly before 12:45 [[Central Standard Time|CST]] (18:45 [[Coordinated Universal Time|UTC]]).<ref name="NBCNEWS">{{cite web |date=February 24, 2019 |orig-date=February 23, 2019 |title=Remains found after cargo jet with three aboard crashes in water near Houston |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/cargo-jet-three-reported-aboard-crashes-water-near-houston-n974981 |access-date=February 23, 2019 |website=NBC News}}</ref><ref name="josephs">{{cite web |last=Josephs |first=Leslie |date=February 23, 2019 |title=Cargo jet flying for Amazon crashes outside of Houston with 3 people aboard, no sign of survivors |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2019/02/23/atlas-air-flight-3591boeing-767-cargo-jet-crashes-near-houston-airport-with-three-people-on-board.html |access-date=February 23, 2019 |website=cnbc.com}}</ref><ref name="auto1">{{Cite web |date=February 24, 2019 |title=Atlas Air Confirms Family Assistance Established in Flight 3591 Accident |url=http://www.atlasairworldwide.com/2019/02/atlas-air-confirms-family-assistance-established-in-flight-3591-accident/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190225161943/https://www.atlasairworldwide.com/2019/02/atlas-air-confirms-family-assistance-established-in-flight-3591-accident/ |archive-date=February 25, 2019 |access-date=February 25, 2019 |website=Atlas Air Worldwide}}</ref> This was the first fatal crash of a Boeing 767 freighter.<ref name="ASN">{{Cite web |last=Ranter |first=Harro |title=ASN Aircraft accident Boeing 767-375ER (BCF) (WL) N1217A Trinity Bay, near Anahuac, TX |url=https://aviation-safety.net/database/record.php?id=20190223-0 |access-date=November 30, 2019 |website=Aviation Safety Network |publisher=[[Flight Safety Foundation]]}}</ref>

Investigators attributed the accident to [[pilot error]], finding that the [[First officer (aviation)|first officer]]{{snd}}who had years of flight performance issues at four previous airlines, but concealed that in his application to Atlas{{snd}}experienced [[spatial disorientation]] and inadvertently placed the aircraft in an unrecoverable dive, while the [[Pilot in command|captain]] failed to adequately monitor the first officer's actions and the flight path of the aircraft. Flight crew training issues at [[Atlas Air]] and across the U.S. commercial aviation industry were also implicated.

== Background ==

=== Aircraft ===

The Boeing 767-375ER({{abbr|BCF|Boeing Converted Freighter}}) ({{abbr|MSN|manufacturer's serial number}} 25865/430) aircraft was registered N1217A and was nearly 27 years old at the time of the accident, having been built in 1992. It was originally ordered by [[Canadian Airlines]], but it was first placed into service by [[China Southern Airlines]] through [[Guinness Peat Aviation|GPA]], an aircraft leasing company.<ref>{{cite web|date=February 25, 2019|title=Amazon Cargo Aircraft Crashes on Flight 3591|url=https://www.aviationcv.com/aviation-blog/2019/amazon-cargo-aircraft-crashes-flight-3591|access-date=February 25, 2019|website=aviationcv.com|archive-date=February 26, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190226111242/https://www.aviationcv.com/aviation-blog/2019/amazon-cargo-aircraft-crashes-flight-3591|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1997, the aircraft was transferred to [[LATAM Chile|LAN Airlines]] and flew until 2014 before being returned to lessor CIT, which then stored it in January 2016. In April 2017, the 767 was converted into a freighter and placed into service for [[Amazon Air]] by Atlas Air.<ref>{{cite web|last=Mollenhauer|first=Alec|date=October 21, 2017|title=Tracking Amazon Prime Air's fleet: aircraft from six continents and 35 airlines|url=https://aeronauticsonline.com/tracking-amazon-prime-airs-fleet-aircraft-from-six-continents/|access-date=February 26, 2019|website=aeronauticsonline.com|archive-date=February 27, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190227060122/https://aeronauticsonline.com/tracking-amazon-prime-airs-fleet-aircraft-from-six-continents/|url-status=usurped}}</ref> In August 2018, Amazon named two aircraft in its fleet, including N1217A as ''CustomAir Obsession''. The name, painted on the aircraft just aft of the cockpit windows, was a near homonym of "customer obsession," an Amazon leadership principle.<ref>{{cite web|title=Leadership Principles|url=https://www.amazon.jobs/en/principles|access-date=February 26, 2019|website=amazon.jobs}}</ref> The aircraft had accumulated more than 91,000 hours across 23,300 flights<ref>{{cite news|date=February 24, 2019|title=[UPDATE 8] Atlas Air Boeing 767 Operating for Amazon Prime Air Crashes|website=Aviation Tribune|url=http://aviationtribune.com/safety/atlas-air-boeing-767-operating-for-amazon-prime-air-crashes/|access-date=February 26, 2019}}</ref><ref name="DCA19MA086">{{Cite web|title=Atlas Air #3591 crashed into Trinity Bay DCA19MA086|url=https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/Pages/DCA19MA086.aspx|access-date=March 13, 2019|website=www.ntsb.gov|publisher=National Transportation Safety Board|id=DCA19MA086}}</ref><ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" /> and was powered by two [[General Electric CF6#CF6-80|GE CF6-80]] turbofan engines.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|pages=8–9}}<ref>{{cite web|title=FAA Registry, N1217A|url=https://registry.faa.gov/AircraftInquiry/NNum_Results.aspx?NNumbertxt=N1217A|access-date=February 25, 2019|publisher=Federal Aviation Administration|archive-date=February 25, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190225223729/https://registry.faa.gov/AircraftInquiry/NNum_Results.aspx?NNumbertxt=N1217A|url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== Crew and passenger ===
There were three people on board the aircraft:<ref name="auto">{{cite web|last=Collman|first=Ashley|title=Breaking news: Boeing 767 cargo plane crashes in Texas, reportedly killing all three on board|url=https://www.thisisinsider.com/atlas-air-cargo-plane-crashes-in-texas-with-three-on-board-2019-2|website=INSIDER}}</ref> Captain Ricky Blakely of [[Indiana]] (60), First Officer Conrad Jules Aska of [[Cedar Grove, Antigua and Barbuda|Cedar Grove]], [[Antigua]] (44), and [[Mesa Airlines]] captain Sean Archuleta of Houston (36; a [[Jump seat|jumpseater]] aboard the flight), who was in his final week of employment at Mesa Airlines and was traveling to work before beginning new-hire pilot training with [[United Airlines]] scheduled for the following week.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Schuetz|first=R. A.|date=February 24, 2019|title=3 confirmed dead after Boeing 767 cargo plane's nose dive into Trinity Bay|url=https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/article/FAA-Cargo-plane-crashed-in-Trinity-By-in-13639542.php|access-date=February 25, 2019|publisher=Houston Chronicle}}</ref>

Blakely joined Atlas Air in 2015 and became a Boeing 767<!-- The Boeing 757 and 767 have the same [[type rating]] despite being different aircraft. --> captain in 2018. Before being hired by Atlas Air, Blakely had previously been an Embraer ERJ-145 captain for [[ExpressJet]]. He had also been a Beechcraft 1900 first officer for [[CommutAir]], and a flight instructor for FlightSafety<!-- The NTSB typed "FlightSafety" as one word in the report. --> International.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|page=5}} Blakely logged a total of 11,172 flight hours, including 1,252 hours on the Boeing 767.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|pages=3–4}}

Aska joined Atlas Air on July 3, 2017, and received his type rating on the Boeing 767 two months later. He had logged 5,073 flight hours, with 520 of them on the 767. Aska had previously been an Embraer E175 first officer with Mesa Airlines (and served with five other airlines prior to that) and also had experience on Embraer's [[Embraer EMB 120 Brasilia|EMB 120 Brasilia]] and ERJ aircraft families.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|pages=5,7}}<ref name="operations">{{Cite web |date=November 19, 2019 |title=Operations Group Chairman's Factual Report |url=https://data.ntsb.gov/Docket/Document/docBLOB?ID=40479145&FileExtension=.PDF&FileName=Operations%20Group%20Chairman%27s%20Factual%20Report-Master.PDF |access-date=December 20, 2019 |publisher=National Transportation Safety Board }}</ref>

Both pilots had previous experience in landing at George Bush Intercontinental Airport<ref name="operations" /> and they flew together on the previous day, operating a night-time flight from California to Miami.<ref name="operations" />

== Accident ==

[[File:Atlas Air Flight 3591 crash site 2.jpg|thumb|Another view of the crash site. The window plugs, which had been installed during the aircraft’s cargo conversion, had blown out on impact with the water.]]

Atlas Air 3591 departed Miami at 10:33 CST (11:33 EST), with First Officer Aska as pilot flying and Captain Blakely pilot monitoring. At 12:36, Aska transferred control of the aircraft to Blakely, telling him that the [[Electronic flight instrument system|electronic flight instrument]] (EFI) switch on his side had malfunctioned. This issue was resolved a minute later, with the following being recorded on the [[cockpit voice recorder]] (CVR):<!--Unless otherwise stated, all information from the CVR that is in this article was transcribed as the NTSB did-->

: Aska: "I press the E-fy<!--Transcribed as said in the CVR transcript--> button, it fixes everything."

: Blakely: "Oh ya ya."

Flight 3591 was on approach towards Houston when it flew through the forward edge of a [[cold front]], which produced an area of [[instrument meteorological conditions]] (IMC) with clouds and [[turbulence]], with cloud tops varying from approximately {{convert|19500|ft|m}} to {{convert|27300|ft|m}} of altitude and cloud bases varying from {{convert|2000|ft|m}} to {{convert|3000|ft|m}} above ground level. The pilot of another nearby airliner reported IMC, and a video taken by a ground witness showed a [[shelf cloud]] passing over the area at the time.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|pages=14–15}} 

Aska then requested radar vectors to the west side of the airport to avoid the inclement weather. The controller accepted but also advised the crew to expedite their descent to {{Convert|3000|ft|m|abbr=}} and said, "I'm gunna get ya west of this weather and northbound for a base leg." Blakely then transferred control of the aircraft back to Aska:

: Aska: "Ok. Two seven zero." 
:
: Blakely: "Your controls." 
:
: Aska: "My controls."

The flight crew then started to configure the aircraft for landing and set up the [[flight management system]] (FMS). At 12:38:02.2 CST, Aska called out "flaps one”, and the slats were extended. Twenty nine seconds later, the aircraft's [[Takeoff/go-around switch|go-around mode]] was inadvertently activated. At 12:38:40.3, the following was heard on the CVR:

: Cockpit area microphone (CAM): [Sound of master caution aural warning]

:Blakely (radio transmission): "Sounds good uh Giant thirty-five ninety-one."

: Approach controller: "It is severe clear on the other side of this stuff so you'll have no problem gettin' the airport [unintelligible word] (either)."<!--the "either" was questionable.-->

: Aska: "Oh. Woah! (Where's) my speed my speed? [Spoken in elevated voice]

: CAM: [Sound similar to a mechanical click]

: Blakely (radio transmission): "Okay."

: Aska: "We're [[Stall (fluid dynamics)|stalling]]! Stall!" [Exclaimed]

: Voice unidentified: "[Expletive]"
  
: Aska: "Lord…you have my soul."

[[File:Atlas Air Flight 3591 FDR simulation.gif|thumb|Reconstruction of the final 20 seconds of the accident sequence]]
The aircraft sharply turned south before going into a rapid descent. Witnesses to the crash described the plane as entering a nosedive; some also recalled hearing "what sounded like lightning" before the Boeing 767 collided with the ground.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Kennedy |first1=Megan |last2=Taylor |first2=Brittany |last3=Aufdenspring |first3=Matt |date=February 23, 2019 |title=3 presumed dead after cargo jet nose-dived into Trinity Bay, sheriff says |url=https://www.click2houston.com/news/boeing-767-cargo-jet-crashes-into-trinity-bay-3-people-aboard-faa-says |access-date=February 23, 2019 |work=KPRC}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://abc13.co/2EsVaGY|title=Witnesses recall moments before Atlas Air cargo plane crash in Chambers Co.|last=Wrigley|first=Deborah|date=February 24, 2019|work=ABC13 Houston|access-date=March 6, 2019}}</ref> 

At 12:36 [[Central Time Zone|CST]] (18:36 [[UTC]]), radar and radio contact was lost. There was no distress call.<ref name="abc13">{{cite news|title=One victim identified in deadly cargo jet crash in Chambers County |url=https://abc13.com/1-victim-identified-in-deadly-cargo-jet-crash-in-chambers-co/5154495/ |work=abc13.com |access-date=February 25, 2019}}</ref> At 12:39:03.9 CST (18:39:03.9 UTC), the time the CVR recording ended, Flight 3591 crashed into the north end of [[Trinity Bay (Texas)|Trinity Bay]] at Jack's Pocket.<ref name="josephs" /> The area of water is within [[Chambers County, Texas]], in proximity to [[Anahuac, Texas|Anahuac]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://abc13.com/witnesses-recall-moments-before-cargo-plane-crash/5153812/abc13.com/5153229/|title=Human remains found after Atlas Air cargo plane crashes in Chambers Co. |publisher=[[KTRK-TV]]|date=February 23, 2019|access-date=February 28, 2019}}</ref>

The [[Federal Aviation Administration]] (FAA) issued an alert after radar and radio contact was lost around {{convert|30|mi|-1||}} southeast of its destination.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Law |first1=Tara |title=Cargo Boeing 767 Plane, Carrying 3, Crashes Into Texas Bay |url=https://time.com/5536049/cargo-plane-crashes-texas-bay-boeing-767/ |magazine=Time |access-date=February 24, 2019}}</ref> Air traffic controllers tried at least twice to contact the flight, with no response. Controllers asked pilots of two nearby flights whether or not they saw a crash site, both of whom said they did not; the crash site was located after ground witnesses called local police to report having seen the aircraft dive into the bay. The [[United States Coast Guard]] dispatched a helicopter and several boats to search for survivors, and other agencies responded. The crash site was mostly mud marsh, with water varying in depth from zero to {{convert|5|ft|spell=in||}} deep, thus [[airboat]]s were needed to access the area. Searchers found human remains and many small fragments of the aircraft and its cargo. The largest recovered piece of the aircraft was {{cvt|50|ft}} in length. The local sheriff described the scene as "total devastation" and surmised that the crash had not been survivable.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Warren|first1=David|last2=Bleiberg|first2=Jake|date=February 24, 2019|title=Sheriff: No likely survivors in jetliner crash near Houston|work=[[Associated Press]]|url=https://www.apnews.com/986ca7a30923439cb8302b2be1da60eb|access-date=February 8, 2021|quote=Witnesses told emergency personnel that the twin-engine plane "went in nose first," leaving a debris field three-quarters of a mile long in Trinity Bay, Chambers County Sheriff Brian Hawthorne said. "It's probably a crash that nobody would survive," he said, referring to the scene as "total devastation."}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://abc13.com/5153229/|title=Human remains found cargo plane crash in Chambers Co.|date=February 23, 2019|work=ABC13 Houston|access-date=February 8, 2021}}</ref>

== Victims ==
On February 24, Atlas Air confirmed that all three people on board died.<ref name="auto1" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hughes |first=Trevor |date=February 24, 2019 |title=Three confirmed dead after Amazon Prime Air cargo plane crash in Texas |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/2019/02/24/amazon-prime-air-cargo-plane-crash-one-body-recovered-search-ongoing/2971795002/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190224232750/https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/2019/02/24/amazon-prime-air-cargo-plane-crash-one-body-recovered-search-ongoing/2971795002/ |archive-date=February 24, 2019 |access-date=February 25, 2019 |website=USA Today |language=en}}</ref> The victims were first identified on social media by friends and family. By February 26, the bodies of all three had been recovered, and by March 4, all had been positively identified.<ref>{{cite web |last=Jordan |first=Jay R. |date=March 4, 2019 |title=Pilot's remains positively identified in deadly Atlas Air cargo plane crash |url=https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/houston/article/Final-remains-positively-identified-in-deadly-13661456.php |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190304233417/https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/houston/article/Final-remains-positively-identified-in-deadly-13661456.php |archive-date=March 4, 2019 |access-date=April 30, 2019 |website=CBS News |publisher=Houston Chronicle}}</ref>

== Investigation ==
[[File:NTSB Trinity Bay Debris (32271873437).jpg|thumb|NTSB investigators examine debris at the edge of Trinity Bay]]
[[File:Atlas Air Flight Recorders (47218247282).jpg|thumb|NTSB investigators recover the flight data recorder from Trinity Bay]]
Investigators from the FAA, [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] (FBI), and [[National Transportation Safety Board]] (NTSB) were dispatched to the accident site with the NTSB leading the accident investigation.<ref name="CNN">{{Cite web |last1=Almasy |first1=Steve |last2=Silverman |first2=Hollie |date=February 23, 2019 |title=Cargo jet with 3 aboard crashes in Texas |url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/02/23/us/texas-atlas-air-cargo-jet-crash/index.html |access-date=February 23, 2019 |website=CNN}}</ref> A dive team from the [[Texas Department of Public Safety]] (DPS) was tasked with locating the aircraft's flight recorders and dive teams from the [[Houston Police Department|Houston]] and [[Baytown, Texas|Baytown]] police departments were also on-scene assisting in the search.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/02/24/us/texas-atlas-air-cargo-jet-crash-sunday/index.html|title=Two bodies recovered after a cargo plane crashes in water near Houston|website=CNN|date=February 24, 2019 |language=en|access-date=February 27, 2019}}</ref> The CVR and [[flight data recorder]] (FDR) were located and transported to an NTSB lab for analysis.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Jasper Scherer |first1=Jacob Dick |title=Black box recovered at Amazon plane crash site in Anahuac |work=Houston Chronicle |date=March 2019 |url=https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/houston/article/Black-box-recovered-at-Amazon-plane-crash-site-in-13656141.php |access-date=March 1, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/03/03/us/texas-cargo-jet-flight-data-recorder/index.html|title=NTSB recovers flight data recorder from cargo plane crash near Houston|last=Vera|first=Amir|date=March 3, 2019|website=CNN|access-date=March 4, 2019}}</ref> It was thought that investigators would likely remain at the accident site for weeks for recovery.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.whec.com/national/boeing-767-cargo-jetliner-with-3-aboard-crashes-near-houston/5256675/|title=Sheriff: No likely survivors in jetliner crash near Houston|date=February 23, 2019|website=WHEC News10NBC|language=en|access-date=February 24, 2019|archive-date=February 24, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190224074823/https://www.whec.com/national/boeing-767-cargo-jetliner-with-3-aboard-crashes-near-houston/5256675/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

It was noted that storm cells were nearby at the time of the accident, but this is not unusual for Bush Intercontinental.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/article/FAA-Cargo-plane-crashed-in-Trinity-By-in-13639542.php|title=Sheriff: 'I don't believe anyone could survive' cargo plane's nose dive into Trinity Bay|last1=Scherer|first1=Jasper|last2=Despart|first2=Zach|date=February 23, 2019|website=Houston Chronicle|access-date=February 24, 2019}}</ref> [[CCTV]] cameras at the Chambers County jail show the airplane in a steep, nose-low descent just prior to impact.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Josephs |first1=Leslie |title=Atlas Air Flight 3591: NTSB starts investigation into cargo jet crash |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2019/02/25/atlas-air-amazon-air-flight-3591-investigation-begins-into-deadly-cargo-jet-crash.html |website=CNBC |date=February 24, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Air disaster Boeing 767-375ER crash in Trinity Bay, near Anahuac, USA |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ZMHeIBBOSg |website=YouTube |date=February 27, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Chron |first1=Jay R. Jordan |last2=Hensley |first2=Nicole |date=2019-03-06 |title=Dramatic video shows final moments as Atlas Air jet plunges into Trinity Bay |url=https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/houston/article/New-video-shows-Atlas-Air-plane-crash-into-13668603.php |access-date=2023-05-27 |website=Chron |language=en-US}}</ref>

The [[FAA]], [[Boeing]], [[Atlas Air]], [[National Air Traffic Controllers Association]] (NATCA), [[International Brotherhood of Teamsters]], [[Air Line Pilots Association, International|Air Line Pilots Association]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.alpa.org/news-and-events/news-room/2019-02-24-atlas-air-flight-3591|title=ALPA Statement on Atlas Air Flight 3591 Accident|website=ALPA|publisher=Air Line Pilots Association|access-date=March 4, 2019}}</ref> and engine maker [[General Electric]] assisted or offered their assistance to the NTSB inquiry.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hemmerdinger |first1=Jon |title=Video shows Atlas 767F in 'steep' dive prior to crash: NTSB |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/video-shows-atlas-767f-in-steep-dive-prior-to-cras-456054/ |website=FlightGlobal.com |access-date=February 25, 2019}}</ref>

After listening to the cockpit voice recorder, the NTSB stated that "Crew communications consistent with a loss of control of the aircraft began approximately 18 seconds prior to the end of the recording."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ntsb.gov/news/press-releases/Pages/mr20190305.aspx|title=NTSB Laboratory Completes Initial Review of Cockpit Voice Recorder, Recovers Flight Data Recorder|date=March 5, 2019|website=www.ntsb.gov|publisher=National Transportation Safety Board|access-date=March 6, 2019}}</ref> On March 12, the NTSB stated that the airplane "pitched nose down over the next 18 seconds to about 49° in response to column input." Later that day, amended its statement to "...in response to nose-down elevator deflection."<ref name="DCA19MA086" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=March 12, 2019 |title=NTSB update on Atlas Air B767 crash: nose pitched down to about 49° 'in response to elevator deflection' |url=https://news.aviation-safety.net/2019/03/12/ntsb-update-on-atlas-air-b767-crash-nose-pitched-down-to-about-49-in-response-to-column-input/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190331131206/https://news.aviation-safety.net/2019/03/12/ntsb-update-on-atlas-air-b767-crash-nose-pitched-down-to-about-49-in-response-to-column-input/ |archive-date=March 31, 2019 |access-date=April 3, 2019 |website=ASN News |publisher=Flight Safety Foundation}}</ref>

On December 19, 2019, the NTSB released a public docket containing over 3,000 pages of factual information it had collected during the investigation, with a final report to follow at an unspecified later date. The docket contains information on "operations, survival factors, human performance, air traffic control, aircraft performance, and includes the cockpit voice recorder transcript, sound spectrum study, and the flight data recorder information."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ntsb.gov/news/press-releases/Pages/NR20191219.aspx|title=NTSB Opens Public Docket for Investigation of Atlas Air Flight 3591 Cargo Plane Crash|website=www.ntsb.gov|publisher=National Transportation Safety Board|access-date=December 19, 2019}}</ref>

On June 11, 2020, the NTSB announced that the next board meeting would determine the cause of the accident;<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-06-11|title=MEDIA ADVISORY: Fatal Atlas Air Flight 3591 Cargo Plane Crash Subject of Board Meeting|url=https://www.ntsb.gov/news/press-releases/Pages/NR20200611.aspx|access-date=2020-06-12|website=www.ntsb.gov|publisher=National Transportation Safety Board}}</ref> 
the NTSB determined during a public board meeting held on July 14, that the flight crashed because of the first officer's inappropriate response to an inadvertent activation of the airplane's go-around mode, resulting in his [[spatial disorientation]] that led him to place the airplane in a steep descent from which the crew did not recover.<ref>{{cite web |title=First Officer, Captain Actions, Aviation Industry Practices, Led to Fatal Atlas Air Crash |url=https://ntsb.gov/news/press-releases/Pages/NR20200714.aspx |website=NTSB |publisher=National Transportation Safety Board |access-date=15 July 2020}}</ref> The NTSB released an animation of the mishap sequence of events from the selection of Go-Around thrust to the fatal crash 31 seconds later.<ref>{{cite web |title=NTSB Animation - Rapid Descent and Crash into Water Atlas Air Inc. Flight 3591 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GsSNr5DR840 |website=Youtube | date=July 14, 2020 |publisher=National Transportation Safety Board |access-date=14 July 2020}}</ref>

===Conclusions===
On August 6, 2020, the NTSB posted the final accident report to their website, which stated: 
{{quote|The  NTSB  determines  that  the  probable  cause  of  this  accident  was  the  inappropriate  response by the first officer as the pilot flying to an inadvertent activation of the go-around mode, which led to his spatial disorientation and nose-down control inputs that placed the airplane in a steep descent from which the crew did not recover. Contributing to the accident was the captain's failure to adequately monitor the airplane's flightpath and assume positive control of the airplane to  effectively  intervene.  Also  contributing  were  systemic  deficiencies  in  the  aviation  industry's selection  and  performance  measurement  practices,  which  failed  to  address  the  first  officer's  aptitude-related  deficiencies  and  maladaptive  stress  response.  Also  contributing  to  the  accident was  the  Federal  Aviation  Administration's  failure  to  implement  the  pilot  records  database  in  a  sufficiently robust and timely manner.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report">{{Cite web|date=2020-07-14|title=Rapid Descent and Crash into Water, Atlas Air Inc. Flight 3591, Boeing 767-375BCF, N1217A, Trinity Bay, Texas, February 23, 2019|url=https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/AccidentReports/Reports/AAR2002.pdf|access-date=2020-08-06|publisher=National Transportation Safety Board|id=NTSB/AAR-20/02}}</ref>|author=|title=|source=}}
The NTSB found that the descent had proceeded normally until the go-around mode was activated and the aircraft's [[autopilot]] and [[autothrottle]] increased engine thrust and nose-up pitch as designed. Neither pilot verbally acknowledged that go-around mode had been actuated nor took any apparent action to deactivate it. Moments later, the first officer made nose-down flight control inputs for stall recovery, but the aircraft's stall warning systems had not activated and FDR data was inconsistent with an aircraft in a stalled condition.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|page=2}} The NTSB concluded that the first officer most likely struck the go-around switch accidentally with his left wrist or his wristwatch while manipulating the nearby [[speedbrake]] lever and that neither pilot realized that the aircraft's automated flight mode had been changed.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|page=ix}} During a stall, established procedures called for the pilot flying (PF) to "Hold the control column firmly", "Disengage the autopilot and autothrottle", and "'''Smoothly''' apply nose-down elevator control to reduce the AOA (angle-of-attack) until stick shaker or buffet stops". The procedures further state that the pilot monitoring (in this case the captain) should monitor and call out changes in altitude / airspeed, call out any trend toward terrain, and verify that all required actions are being completed.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|pages=vii,27}} While the first officer's flight control inputs were aggressive enough to override the autopilot,<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|page=20}} investigators concluded that the captain was distracted performing other tasks and had failed to monitor the aircraft's performance.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|pages=42–43}}

The NTSB concluded that the aircraft was likely flying in [[Instrument meteorological conditions|IMC]] without the ground visible when the go-around mode was activated,<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|page=41}} and the first officer most likely experienced a pitch-up or head-up [[somatogravic illusion]], the false sensation that one is tilting backwards during unexpected forward acceleration in the absence of visible landmarks. Pilots with limited [[Instrument flight rules|instrument flight]] proficiency have a well-documented tendency to disregard flight instruments and act instinctively in reaction to this illusion.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|pages=ix, 40-41}} Investigators concluded that the pilots were unable to see the ground until the aircraft exited the clouds approximately {{convert|3000|ft|m}} above the bay, at which point safe recovery from the steep descent would have been impossible.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|pages=44–45}}

The NTSB was unable to determine why the first officer cycled the EFI switch prior to the accident; however, cycling the EFI switch in the 767 is generally done to solve intermittent display blanking and does not change the source of the data shown on the display, and the NTSB concluded that "whatever EFIS display anomaly the FO [first officer] experienced was resolved to both crewmembers' satisfaction (by the 
FO's cycling of the EFI  switch) before the events related to the accident sequence occurred."<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|page=37}}

===Flight crew training issues===
The NTSB noted that both pilots had difficulties in their training. Blakely experienced difficulties during training for his [[type rating]] on the 767. On October 31, 2015, he was declared unfit for a [[FAA Practical Test|checkride]]<!-- The NTSB typed "checkride" as one word in the report. --> due to unsatisfactory remarks on his training which included the following:<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|page=4}}

* Allowing airspeed to exceed flap limits during stall recovery training
* Forgetting to set the missed approach altitude
* Difficulties in performing missed approaches

Blakely underwent remedial training the next day on November 1, this time with satisfactory results. The day after, he had his 767 checkride, and received his type rating on the aircraft two days later.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" /><ref name="operations" /> Despite Blakely's improvements, Atlas Air placed him in the pilot proficiency watch program (PWP) due to his training issues.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />

First officer Aska had also experienced training difficulties with Atlas Air, more so than Blakely. According to the NTSB, Aska had been unable to complete pilot training at two other airlines, which he did not disclose on his job applications to Atlas.<ref name="Levin" /> The NTSB found that Aska had a "long history of training performance deficiencies", with a "tendency to respond impulsively and inappropriately when faced with an unexpected event during training scenarios".<ref>{{Cite web |last=O'Connor |first=Kate |date=2020-07-16 |title=NTSB Cites Pilot Performance In Atlas Air Crash |url=https://www.avweb.com/flight-safety/accidents-ntsb/ntsb-cites-pilot-performance-in-atlas-air-crash/ |access-date=2025-02-01 |website=AVweb}}</ref> Aska's first issues at Atlas emerged in July 2017, the same month he joined the airline, when he was declined an oral exam for his type rating on the 767 as he needed remediation training. Following the training, he passed the oral exam. Aska then went through five fixed-base (non-moving) [[flight simulator]] sessions, experiencing difficulties with normal procedures, and underwent more remediation training. In August, following two full-flight simulator training sessions, Aska's simulator partner complained that he was being "held back." Atlas Air ultimately had to restart full-flight simulator training for Aska because no other pilots remained in his training class to partner with him.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report"/>{{Reference page|pages=5–6}}

Aska's first checkride on the aircraft ended in failure due to poor [[crew resource management]] (CRM) and improper aircraft control. His examiner described him as stressed and lacking [[situational awareness]].<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|page=6}} Aska underwent remedial training on September 25 and the next day, he reattempted his checkride successfully, receiving his type rating on the aircraft.<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />

The NTSB concluded that Aska had been able to conceal his spotty training record because of shortcomings in the FAA pilot records database, and criticized the FAA for failing to upgrade the database earlier. A 2010 amendment to the [[Pilot Record Improvement Act]] (PRIA) passed after the 2009 crash of [[Colgan Air Flight 3407]] required the FAA to record training failures in the database; however, this provision had not been fully implemented due to privacy concerns and industry opposition, particularly from [[business aviation]] operators who objected to the program's stringent record-keeping requirements. Atlas Air was also criticized for its reliance on agents rather than flight operations specialists to check the training backgrounds of pilots it hired.<ref>{{cite web |last=Kaminski-Morrow |first=David |date=October 29, 2020 |title=How Atlas freighter crash revived scrutiny of pilot performance tracking |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/flight-international/how-atlas-freighter-crash-revived-scrutiny-of-pilot-performance-tracking/140771.article |access-date=January 13, 2021 |website=[[FlightGlobal]]}}</ref> Atlas Air's director of training said they would not have hired Aska if they had known his full training record.<ref name="Levin">{{Cite magazine |last=Levin |first=Alan |date=2019-12-20 |title=Pilot in Amazon Cargo Plane Crash Repeatedly Flunked Flight Tests |url=https://time.com/5753435/amazon-atlas-air-cargo-crash/# |access-date=2025-02-01 |magazine=TIME}}</ref> 

The NTSB recommended that pilots of the 767 and the similar [[Boeing 757]] be trained to recognize and recover from inadvertent go-around mode actuation, but also concluded that available data suggested that such an actuation was a "rare and typically benign event."<ref name="AAR-20-02 Final Report" />{{Reference page|page=viii}}

The crash of Atlas Air Flight 3591 was featured in the 2023 episode "[[List of Mayday episodes#ep209|Delivery to Disaster]]", of the Canadian-made, internationally distributed documentary series ''[[Mayday (Canadian TV series)|Mayday]]''.<ref name=Mayday>{{Cite episode |title=Delivery to Disaster |episode-link=List of Mayday episodes#ep209 |series=[[Mayday (Canadian TV series)|Mayday]] |publisher=[[Cineflix]] |publication-place=Montreal |network=[[Discovery Channel (Canadian TV channel)|Discovery Channel Canada]] et al<!--- per country of origin, article is about the airplane incident - not an exposé of all the permutations and combinations of the Cineflex production: other channels, in other countries, using other series names/episode titles, are found at the linked articles ---> |season=23 |number=9 |date=2023-02-28}}</ref>

extract:
Atlas Air Flight 3591 was a scheduled domestic cargo flight between Miami International Airport and George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston. On February 23, 2019, the Boeing 767 operating this flight crashed into Trinity Bay during approach into Houston, killing the two crew members and single passenger on board. The accident occurred near Anahuac, Texas, east of Houston, shortly before 12:45 CST (18:45 UTC). This was the first fatal crash of a Boeing 767 freighter.
Investigators attributed the accident to pilot error, finding that the first officer – who had years of flight performance issues at four previous airlines, but concealed that in his application to Atlas – experienced spatial disorientation and inadvertently placed the aircraft in an unrecoverable dive, while the captain failed to adequately monitor the first officer's actions and the flight path of the aircraft. Flight crew training issues at Atlas Air and across the U.S. commercial aviation industry were also implicated.
